description: Believing `col = NULL` matches rows where col is NULL, missing that comparing with NULL yields unknown so no row is returned and IS NULL is required.
Believing `col <> 'x'` also returns rows where col is NULL, missing that the NULL rows evaluate to unknown and are filtered out.
Believing NOT IN behaves like the negation of a membership test when the list contains NULL, missing that it then returns no rows at all.
Believing a WHERE clause keeps rows whose condition is unknown, rather than only rows where the condition is true.
Believing AND binds looser than OR, so `a OR b AND c` is read as `(a OR b) AND c` instead of `a OR (b AND c)`.
Believing LIKE with an unescaped `_` or `%` in the pattern matches those characters literally rather than as wildcards.
Believing INNER JOIN keeps rows with no match on the other side, as LEFT JOIN does.
Believing a join on a non-unique column returns one row per left row, missing that each match produces another row and the result multiplies.
Believing a filter on the right table in WHERE leaves a LEFT JOIN unchanged, missing that it discards the NULL-extended rows and turns it into an inner join.
Believing a filter placed in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN removes left rows, rather than only controlling which right rows match.
Believing a join without an ON condition or WHERE returns the matching rows, missing that it produces the Cartesian product of both tables.
Believing a join compares NULL keys as equal, so rows with NULL in both join columns are paired.
Believing COUNT(col) counts every row, missing that it skips rows where col is NULL while COUNT(*) counts all rows.
Believing SUM and AVG treat NULL as zero, so AVG divides by the total row count instead of the count of non-NULL values.
Believing an aggregate over an empty set returns 0, missing that SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX return NULL while COUNT returns 0.
Believing an aggregate function can be used in WHERE to filter groups, rather than in HAVING.
Believing HAVING filters individual rows before grouping, rather than groups after aggregation.
Believing a column not in GROUP BY and not aggregated can be selected, with the database picking the first or only value.
Believing GROUP BY sorts its output, so an ORDER BY is unnecessary to get a guaranteed order.
Believing a scalar subquery that returns more than one row quietly uses the first row, rather than raising an error.
Believing a scalar subquery that returns no rows yields an error, missing that it evaluates to NULL.
Believing an uncorrelated subquery is rerun for each outer row, or that a correlated subquery is evaluated only once.
Believing EXISTS depends on the values the subquery selects, so `EXISTS (SELECT NULL ...)` is false.
Believing UNION keeps duplicate rows, missing that it removes them and UNION ALL is needed to keep them.
Believing UNION matches columns by name, rather than by position and compatible type.
Believing INTERSECT and EXCEPT are order-insensitive, so `A EXCEPT B` equals `B EXCEPT A`.
Believing set operators treat NULLs as distinct, so duplicate NULL rows are kept by UNION and INTERSECT.
Believing a query without ORDER BY returns rows in insertion or primary key order.
Believing a window function collapses rows like GROUP BY, rather than returning one value per input row.
Believing a window function can be filtered in the same query's WHERE clause, missing that it is computed after WHERE and needs a subquery or CTE.
Believing RANK gives consecutive numbers after ties, missing that it leaves gaps while DENSE_RANK does not and ROW_NUMBER never ties.
Believing a window ORDER BY with the default frame gives the whole-partition total, missing that it makes SUM a running total up to the current row's peers.
Believing a non-recursive CTE can reference itself, or that a CTE can be referenced by an earlier sibling in the WITH list.
Believing an UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause affects no rows, rather than every row in the table.
Believing INSERT with a column list can omit a NOT NULL column that has no default.
Believing a UNIQUE constraint rejects more than one NULL, rather than allowing multiple NULLs.
Believing a PRIMARY KEY can contain NULL, or that a table may have several primary keys.
Believing a FOREIGN KEY forces the referencing column to be non-NULL, rather than allowing NULL to mean no reference.
Believing a CHECK constraint rejects a row whose condition evaluates to unknown, missing that only false is rejected.
Believing a foreign key lets you delete the referenced parent row, with child rows quietly kept, when the default action is to reject the delete.
